title: Chest pain and breathlessness three days after a bad meal

source.citation: Mangeshkar S, Borkowski P, Shokrekhuda A, Barillas-Lara MI, Menegus MA. Boerhaave syndrome: an unusual myocardial infarction mimic-a case report. Eur Heart J Case Rep. 2024;8(7):ytae310.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Chest pain, shortness of breath and profound weakness for 3 days
presentation.hpi: Previously well. Three days ago he ate seafood and then had several bouts of forceful vomiting and one episode of diarrhoea. Since then chest pain and breathlessness have crept in, with fatigue and pain in the back and upper abdomen, all worsening steadily up to today, when he feels profoundly weak.

exam: Severe tachypnoea and hypoxia; saturation does not improve appreciably on a non-rebreather mask
Diminished breath sounds over the left lower and mid zones

imaging.modality: CT angiogram chest, abdomen and pelvis
imaging.finding: Large left hydropneumothorax with rightward mediastinal shift concerning for tension physiology; oesophageal wall thickening; no pericardial effusion; no coronary calcification
Contrast leaks into the left pleural space, confirming oesophageal perforation
Normal wall motion; signs of volume depletion
Thickened, inflamed pericardium and pericardial fat consistent with pericarditis

ecg: Diffuse ST-segment elevation, most marked in V1–V5; at discharge, sinus rhythm with resolution of the ST elevation

diagnosis.primary: Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous oesophageal rupture) with purulent left hydropneumothorax and secondary myopericarditis mimicking acute myocardial infarction

management: Non-rebreather oxygen, without appreciable improvement in saturation
Emergency left chest tube: 1600 mL of purulent fluid drained, after which saturation improved

Cardiology consultation: ST elevation and troponin attributed to myopericarditis from the oesophageal leak rather than ischaemia (no coronary calcification, no coronary risk factors); cleared for surgery
Operating room: endoscopy and repair of the oesophageal perforation with an intercostal muscle flap and intercostal nerve cryoablation
Later in the admission: oesophageal stent and jejunal feeding tube, both eventually removed
outcome: Recovered; ECG at discharge showed sinus rhythm with resolution of the ST elevation, and at follow-up he was eating well and gaining weight without complaints.
teachingPoints: Chest, back or upper abdominal pain after forceful vomiting is oesophageal rupture until proven otherwise; Mackler's triad (vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema) is often incomplete.
Distal ruptures usually tear the left posterolateral wall and spill into the left pleura: a left effusion or hydropneumothorax after vomiting is a key clue.

Leaked oesophageal contents can inflame the pericardium and myocardium, producing diffuse ST elevation and a troponin rise that mimic STEMI; normal wall motion and a flat troponin argue against infarction.
CT with water-soluble oral contrast confirms the leak; treatment is nil by mouth, fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, drainage and early source control.
Outcome worsens steeply when treatment is delayed beyond about 24 hours; reflex antiplatelets, heparin or thrombolysis for the ECG can cause harm.

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.extra: ECG: diffuse ST elevation, most marked in V1–V5. Troponin I 0.41 ng/mL (cut-off 0.03).
options: Anterior STEMI complicated by acute left heart failure
Massive pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain
Oesophageal rupture with spillage into the left pleural space
Acute type A aortic dissection involving the coronary ostia
questions.explanation: Pain that began after forceful vomiting, with refractory hypoxia and one-sided loss of breath sounds on the left, points to a distal oesophageal (Boerhaave) rupture draining into the left pleura. A STEMI explains neither the vomiting trigger nor the unilateral chest signs; here the ST changes came from myopericardial inflammation.

questions.q: What best explains the ST elevation and troponin rise?
questions.extra: CT angiogram: large left hydropneumothorax, oesophageal thickening, no pericardial effusion, no coronary calcification. Oral-contrast CT: leak into the left pleural space. Repeat troponin flat; bedside echo: normal wall motion.
options: Myopericardial inflammation from leaked oesophageal contents
Type 1 infarction from an occluded left anterior descending artery
Type 2 infarction from hypoxia on fixed coronary stenoses
questions.explanation: Diffuse ST elevation with normal wall motion, a flat troponin and no coronary calcification fit myopericarditis from mediastinal and pleural contamination, which a later CT confirmed as an inflamed, thickened pericardium. A coronary occlusion or takotsubo would cause regional wall-motion abnormalities.

questions.q: After the chest tube drains 1600 mL of pus, which plan is most appropriate?
questions.extra: Oral-contrast CT: contrast leaks from the distal oesophagus into the left pleural space. Troponin I flat at 0.41 ng/mL; echo shows normal wall motion.
options: Aspirin, ticagrelor and heparin, then coronary angiography before surgery
Nil by mouth, IV antibiotics and a repeat contrast swallow in 48 hours
Antibiotics and intrapleural fibrinolytics for a complicated parapneumonic effusion
Nil by mouth, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical repair
questions.explanation: A non-contained rupture with purulent pleural contamination, presenting days late, needs source control (drainage plus surgical or endoscopic repair) alongside nil by mouth, fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (WSES 2019 guidelines on oesophageal emergencies). Antiplatelets and heparin for a presumed ACS add bleeding risk without benefit; watchful waiting suits only small contained leaks in stable patients.

evidence.quote: A 52-year-old male with no pertinent medical history presented to the emergency department with 3 days of chest pain, shortness of breath, and profound weakness.
The patient ate seafood 3 days prior, after which he experienced several bouts of forceful vomiting and an episode of diarrhoea.
he noticed insidious onset of chest pain and shortness of breath accompanied by fatigue and back and upper abdominal pain, which significantly worsened until presentation
severely tachypnoeic with respiratory rate nearly 40 b.p.m. and hypoxic with oxygen saturation in the range of 80–85% on room air
Cardiovascular exam was notable for a heart rate of 120 b.p.m. with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg.
Respiratory system examination revealed diminished breath sounds on the left-sided lower and mid-lung. There were no other pertinent physical exam findings.
The patient was immediately placed on a non-rebreather mask without appreciable increase in oxygen saturation.
revealed a large left hydropneumothorax with a right mediastinal shift concerning for tension physiology along with some oesophageal thickening
but there was no evidence of pericardial effusion
A chest tube was placed emergently and drained 1600 mL of purulent fluid after which the oxygen saturation showed improvement.
Intravenous fluids and antibiotics were initiated.
A chest CT with oral contrast revealed leakage of contrast into the left pleural space confirming an oesophageal perforation
ECG showed diffuse ST segment elevations
Initial electrocardiogram showing ST segment elevations, particularly demonstrable in leads V1–V5.
troponin I was also elevated with a peak of 0.41 ng/mL (normal cut-off: 0.03 ng/mL)
Serial troponin levels were stable without a rising trend, consistent with myocardial injury rather than infarction.
less likely due to ischaemic involvement but rather could be explained by inflammation of the myo-pericardium secondary to leakage of oesophageal contents
absence of coronary calcifications on the chest CT scan and lack of overt risk factors for coronary disease
A bedside echocardiogram showed normal wall motion with evidence of volume depletion
underwent an endoscopy with successful repair of the oesophageal perforation using an intercostal muscle flap with intercostal nerve cryoablation
demonstrated thickened and inflamed pericardium and pericardial fat, consistent with pericarditis
the patient needed an oesophageal stent placement and a jejunal tube placement with eventual removal of both
diagnosed with Boerhaave syndrome complicated by myopericarditis, although the presentation was concerning for acute coronary syndrome
The ECG at discharge showed normal sinus rhythm with resolution of previously noted ST segment elevations.
the patient was seen to be eating well, gaining weight without any further complaints
